laws: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) §351 (criminal intimidation); Indian Penal Code (IPC) §506 (criminal intimidation); IPC §352 (assault or use of criminal force); IPC §166 (misconduct by public servant); Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNSS) §218 (sanction for prosecution of public servants); Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) §§200, 203 (private complaint to magistrate).
sections_applied: BNS 351; IPC 506; IPC 352; IPC 166; BNSS 218; CrPC 200; CrPC 203.
precedents: Supreme Court judgment clarifying the elements of criminal intimidation under Section 506 IPC (intent to cause alarm required). No judicial authority was retrieved for assault, misconduct by public servant, or the procedural requirement of prior sanction under BNSS 218. All other materials are secondary (legal blogs).

issues: Does the SHO's threat to place the complainant in lock‑up constitute criminal intimidation?
Does the act of pushing a paper amount to assault or use of criminal force?
Can the SHO be charged with misconduct/abuse of power under IPC 166?
Is prior governmental sanction required before prosecuting the SHO under BNSS 218?
Can the complainant file a direct complaint before the magistrate without police action?
applicable_law: IPC §352 (assault or use of criminal force)
BNSS §218 (sanction for prosecution of public servants)

precedent_analysis.claim: The SHO's threat to lock up the complainant if he withdraws his complaint satisfies the element of intent to cause alarm required for criminal intimidation under BNS §351 / IPC 506.
Pushing a paper constitutes assault or use of criminal force under IPC §352.
The SHO's alleged threat and abuse of power amount to misconduct by a public servant under IPC §166.
Prosecution of the SHO for any of the above offences requires prior sanction of the government under BNSS §218.
The complainant may file a private complaint directly before the magistrate under CrPC §200/§203 when the police refuse to register an FIR.

application: If the threat is proven, the SHO can be charged under BNS 351/IPC 506; the Supreme Court’s clarification that intent to cause alarm is essential supports this charge.
A minimal physical act such as pushing a paper may not meet the threshold of "use of criminal force" required under IPC 352, making the assault charge uncertain.
Misconduct under IPC 166 hinges on whether the SHO acted in the discharge of official duties; the allegation suggests personal motive, which could satisfy the provision.
Even if any of the substantive offences are established, BNSS 218 mandates that the government first grant sanction before a court can take cognizance.
Should the police refuse to register an FIR, the complainant can approach the magistrate directly under CrPC §§200‑203, bypassing the police.
uncertainties: The factual matrix is disputed; the SHO denies any threat or physical contact, leaving the existence of intimidation and assault unproven.
No judicial precedent was found on the application of BNSS 218 to police officers in intimidation cases; the requirement of sanction remains based solely on statutory language.
The threshold for "use of criminal force" in the context of pushing a paper is unclear without case law.
Whether the magistrate can entertain a private complaint for offences that are ordinarily cognizable and police‑investigated may depend on jurisdiction‑specific practice.
